meta.title: World landmark trees outside Europe — wave two strict-gate research

import.warning: Draft import is not human editorial approval. Recheck current access before travel; do not re-import these rows.

meta.decision: Stopped at 24 rather than pad. Every include is a named living individual outside Europe with a sourced event or cultural story, current standing/access evidence, an exact coordinate basis and all-high confidence.
meta.score_contract: Minimum 19/25; story and walkability each at least 4/5.
meta.source_contract: At least two useful sources per include, with a land manager, government, heritage authority or other first-party authority for the story/status and an exact-point basis.
meta.access_contract: Specific living individual only; formal public path, ticketed public garden, managed sacred precinct, public park or safe public visibility. No climbing, barrier crossing or root-zone shortcuts.
meta.dedupe_contract: Normalised primary names and listed aliases checked globally against all 17,131 live catalogue rows and the earlier dossiers; global nearest-neighbour and internal candidate distance checked at 120 m.

missing_city_requirements.rule: Historical proposal provenance. The 17 required objects and flCO entries were applied through the reviewed discovery-wave-2 city plan before draft import.

included.a: Memorial Plaza, 180 Greenwich Street, New York, NY
included.s: the pear tree carried out of Ground Zero and brought back
included.q: 9/11 Survivor Tree New York United States
included.w: Workers found this Callery pear alive but badly burned beneath the World Trade Center wreckage. New York City Parks nursed it back and returned it in 2010; today it stands in the Memorial Plaza as a living witness whose seedlings travel to communities after later tragedies.
included.age_claim: Planted in the 1970s; recovered after 11 September 2001
facts: Recovery workers found the damaged tree at Ground Zero in October 2001.
The rehabilitated tree returned to the memorial site in 2010.
The outdoor Memorial is free and posts daily opening hours.

access.evidence: Free outdoor Memorial Plaza during posted daily hours; the tree is beside the South Pool.
access.safety_filter: Stay on the memorial paving and outside the protected bed; do not touch, climb or cross barriers.

included.a: 620 North Harvey Avenue, Oklahoma City, OK
included.s: the elm left standing after the 1995 bombing
included.q: Oklahoma City Survivor Tree Oklahoma United States
included.w: An American elm that shaded the old parking lot survived the blast that destroyed the Murrah building. The Memorial made it a central emblem of endurance: approach across the outdoor grounds and look back from the rescued tree toward the empty chairs.
local_aliases: Survivor Tree at Oklahoma City National Memorial
included.age_claim: About 100 years old
facts: The elm was the only tree in the immediate area to survive the 19 April 1995 bombing.
Investigators nearly removed it while recovering evidence, but it was preserved.
The tree stands within the freely accessible Outdoor Symbolic Memorial.

access.evidence: Reached on the National Park Service self-guided outdoor memorial route.
access.safety_filter: Use the formal paths and protected viewing space; do not enter the root bed or climb.

included.a: 507 Baylor Street, Austin, TX
included.s: the poisoned live oak that Austin refused to lose
included.q: Austin Treaty Oak Texas United States
included.w: This fenced remnant of an old live-oak grove became a city symbol after deliberate Velpar poisoning in 1989. An extraordinary rescue saved part of its crown; a later vandal hacked at it again, yet the surviving oak still makes this tiny park a charged urban detour.
included.age_claim: Commonly described as several centuries old
facts: The oak was deliberately poisoned with the herbicide Velpar in 1989.
Arborists saved roughly one-third of the original tree.
A further vandalism incident was documented in March 2024.

access.evidence: Visible from the small City of Austin park and included in a 2026 public walking outing.
access.safety_filter: Remain outside the protective fence and root zone; no touching or climbing.

included.s: a park-sized live oak saved by a newspaper legend
included.q: Jacksonville Treaty Oak Florida United States
included.w: Reporter Pat Moran coined the 'Treaty Oak' story in the 1930s to make Jacksonville protect this immense live oak. Philanthropist Jessie Ball duPont then bought and donated the land, leaving a strange case where an invented legend achieved a very real conservation result.
local_aliases: Treaty Oak at Jessie Ball duPont Park
included.age_claim: City estimates place it at roughly 250 years
facts: The treaty story was created by journalist Pat Moran in the 1930s.
Jessie Ball duPont acquired and donated the land around the tree in 1964.
Jacksonville maintains the tree in a public urban park.

access.evidence: The City of Jacksonville lists Jessie Ball duPont Park as the public setting for the tree.
access.safety_filter: Use the open lawn and paths but keep off low limbs and the root zone; no climbing.

included.a: Hampton University, 100 East Queen Street, Hampton, VA
included.s: the campus oak where freedom was taught and proclaimed
included.q: Emancipation Oak Hampton Virginia United States
included.w: Mary Smith Peake taught newly freed people beneath this oak in 1861, before a school building existed. In 1863, local African Americans gathered here for the first Southern reading of the Emancipation Proclamation—a history still rooted near Hampton University's entrance.
included.age_claim: Standing before the Civil War
facts: Mary Smith Peake held classes for freed people beneath the tree in 1861.
A public reading of the Emancipation Proclamation took place under it in 1863.
The tree stands on Hampton University's historic campus near the entrance.

included.w: Local legend says Colonel William Jackson deeded this oak—and the ground within eight feet of it—to the tree itself. The original fell in 1942; Athenians planted one of its acorns here in 1946, so today's living landmark is both offspring and legal folk tale.

included.age_claim: Current descendant planted in 1946
facts: The deed story is a local legend rather than a surviving legal instrument.

facts: President Calvin Coolidge designated it the Nation's Christmas Tree in 1926.

included.s: a banyan that survived the loss of its own main trunk

included.w: An immense ginkgo rises beside Yongmunsa with stories tying it to the last Silla crown prince, a king's staff and a mysterious survival during war. The final approach is a gentle temple walk, letting the tree appear gradually rather than as a roadside specimen.
included.age_claim: Traditionally estimated at more than 1,000 years
facts: South Korea protects the tree as a Natural Monument.
Multiple recorded legends explain its planting and survival.
The tree is reached on the public walking approach to Yongmunsa temple.

access.evidence: Open year-round according to current visitor listings; temple admission or seasonal controls may apply.
access.safety_filter: Use the signed temple path, observe worship etiquette and stay outside the trunk/root enclosure.

included.a: Waipoua Forest, State Highway 12, Northland
included.s: the forest lord reached by a protected kauri walk
included.q: Tāne Mahuta Waipoua Forest New Zealand
included.w: New Zealand's largest known living kauri carries the name of the Māori forest god and stands as a taonga in Waipoua. The encounter is intentionally controlled: a short boardwalk, hygiene station and daily managed hours protect the tree from kauri dieback.
included.age_claim: Commonly estimated at roughly 1,250–2,500 years
facts: The Department of Conservation identifies Tāne Mahuta as New Zealand's largest known living kauri.
The track reopened with a blessing in December 2024 after protective work.
DOC's March 2026 release says Tāne Mahuta remains open while other Waipoua kauri walks close.

access.evidence: DOC's live project page posts daily managed opening hours of 09:00–16:00; conditions can change.
access.safety_filter: Use the cleaning station and boardwalk exactly as directed; never leave the path or touch kauri roots/trunk.

included.a: Burma Road, Pemberton, WA
included.s: a living karri fitted out as a former fire lookout
included.q: Gloucester Tree Pemberton Western Australia
included.w: Foresters once climbed metal pegs spiralling around this giant living karri to watch for bushfires from a platform high above the canopy. Climbing is closed, but the grounded encounter is now more honest: a forest walk to an extraordinary tree carrying the infrastructure of another era.
included.age_claim: Mature karri selected as a lookout in 1947
facts: Foresters selected the tree as a fire lookout in 1947.
Metal climbing pegs and the high platform remain part of the tree's visible history.
The land manager currently prohibits climbing while retaining public ground-level access.

access.evidence: DBCA's current site page provides public trail and facility information; the tree is ground-view only.
access.safety_filter: Do not climb the pegs or cross closures; check DBCA alerts and follow forest-fire restrictions.

included.a: Hilltop Road, Walpole, WA
included.s: a living red tingle hollowed by centuries of fire
included.q: Giant Tingle Tree Walpole Western Australia
included.w: Fire has hollowed an enormous arch through the base of this living red tingle without killing its outer growth layers. A short forest loop and boardwalk let you read the tree's survival from every angle without repeating the old damage caused by walking through it.
included.age_claim: Ancient mature red tingle; no precise age retained
facts: Repeated fire hollowed the living trunk while outer growth remained viable.
DBCA routes visitors around the tree on an 800-metre Class 2 loop.
The current layout protects the trunk and roots from direct foot traffic.

access.evidence: Reached on DBCA's 800 m Class 2 loop from Hilltop Road.
access.safety_filter: Stay on the boardwalk/formal track, never enter the hollow and check fire or road closures.

included.a: Flinders Ranges Way, Ikara–Flinders Ranges National Park, SA
included.s: the river red gum photographed as the Spirit of Endurance
included.q: Cazneaux Tree Ikara Flinders Ranges Australia
included.w: Photographer Harold Cazneaux made this river red gum the subject of his 1937 image 'Spirit of Endurance', turning its contorted survival in dry country into an Australian visual emblem. A signed walking trail now reconnects the photograph to the living subject.
included.age_claim: Mature tree photographed in 1937
facts: Harold Cazneaux photographed the tree in 1937 as Spirit of Endurance.
South Australia records it as a significant tree in Ikara–Flinders Ranges National Park.
A Grade 2 return walk leads to the tree from the Wilpena area.

access.evidence: Reached on the land manager's signed Grade 2 walking route; park entry and seasonal heat conditions apply.
access.safety_filter: Carry water, avoid extreme heat, remain on the trail and never climb or damage the tree.
